routes.description: Establish that the surviving manuscript tradition and textual-critical comparison support a probabilistic recovery of the New Testament authors' wording in essential respects, despite localized uncertainty.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the available witnesses, branching transmission, variant profile, and reconstruction practices jointly warrant substantial textual confidence without requiring certainty in every disputed place.

motionBridge.description: Show that substantial probabilistic recovery of authorial wording is sufficient for responsible trust in the New Testament text.

centralBridges.description: Show that manuscripts, early versions, patristic citations, and multiple transmission lines provide cumulative evidence for reconstructing earlier wording.
Show that most variants are substantively trivial and that the smaller meaningful and viable subset leaves the text substantially recoverable.
Show that extant readings and critical methods ordinarily preserve and identify the authors' wording rather than merely an unrelated later textual state.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend a moderate historical-probability standard instead of requiring certainty unavailable for other ancient texts.
Explain why ordinary scholarly reliance on stable wording supports the practical adequacy of substantial textual recovery.

routes.description: Establish that reconstructing the earliest text represented by surviving witnesses does not sufficiently establish the authors' original wording because consequential changes may predate the extant evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the missing early transmission history, consequential variants, and distinction between initial and original text leave the degree of autographic continuity insufficiently warranted for textual trust.

motionBridge.description: Show that unresolved uncertainty about pre-survival copying prevents the affirmative burden of warranted trust from being met.

centralBridges.description: Show that the long interval before the earliest useful surviving witnesses leaves copying quality, exemplars, and early alterations undocumented.
Show that recovery of the common ancestor behind surviving witnesses does not by itself identify that initial text with an author's original.
Show that meaningful variants and irrecoverable readings remain important even when most observed differences are minor and doctrines remain stable.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why numerous predominantly late witnesses can improve comparative reconstruction without proving preservation of the original wording.
Specify why the advocate of textual trust must supply affirmative evidence of early continuity rather than rely on the absence of demonstrable corruption.

sections.title: Standard and Burden for Textual Trust
sections.rationale: The appropriate threshold—certainty, relative confidence, or substantial recovery in essential respects—determines what the evidence must establish and how residual uncertainty bears on the motion.

sections.title: Early Transmission and the Missing-Witness Gap
sections.rationale: The undocumented interval between composition and the earliest useful witnesses is central to whether branching circulation and indirect evidence warrant continuity or leave consequential alteration unknowable.

sections.title: Witness Abundance, Dating, and Independence
sections.rationale: The quantity, age, distribution, and dependence of manuscripts, versions, and citations determine how much comparative evidential force the surviving witness base provides.

sections.title: Frequency and Significance of Textual Variants
sections.rationale: The principal clash requires distinguishing raw variant totals and trivial differences from meaningful, viable, historically important, or potentially lost early alterations.

sections.title: Critical Reconstruction, Initial Text, and Original Wording
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether textual-critical methods recover authorial wording with adequate probability or only reconstruct an earliest attainable text whose relationship to the autograph remains uncertain.
